title: A Working Holiday Year in Japan: Preparation, Costs, and a Life That Isn't Mostly Working
abstract: From 2025 to 2026 I spent a year on a working holiday in Japan. This post covers prep, what I actually spent, Japanese ability, packing and insurance, and the fact that most of my time wasn't spent on paid work but on work exchange. It's for people who are about to go but hesitating or don't know where to start, and for anyone curious about a less conventional way of living.
text: From mid-June 2025 to mid-June 2026, I was on a working holiday in Japan, and I stayed the whole year. Before leaving, my one wish was to try skiing while working, and beyond that, to experience whatever I hadn't done before, as long as the travel distance wasn't too crazy. There are already plenty of posts online about the preparation process. What I want to share here is what I actually spent, how my time split between work and play, and a few lessons learned, for people still deciding whether to go (worried about money), and for people who've decided but don't know where to start. A working holiday: is it a "holiday" or "work"? The purpose of the visa is mainly a "holiday", and it allows you to work to top up your travel funds and support your life. But in most of the posts I've read from people who did it, something like 80 to 90% of the time was spent working, and they only traveled on days off, between two jobs, or right before going home. Working in Japan also really only covers everyday costs, and you can't save much. Take my three and a half months at a ski resort hotel (12/20 to 3/31): The hourly wage was 1,300 yen. After tax (20.42%) and national health insurance, working 22 days a month, 8 hours a day, that came to about NT$36,000 a month, or about NT$205 an hour. That's close to Taiwan's current minimum wage of NT$196 an hour. Work was shift-based and actual hours went up and down with the number of guests. Over the three and a half months, my pay was NT$8,000, 33,000, 22,000 and 16,000. The dorm was free, thank goodness, though late in the season it often had no hot water, which was painful. Time-clock record for February For me, if there were nothing to gain besides money (learning to ski, practicing Japanese, making friends, experiencing life in snow country), and I were only working to earn a living or travel money, it wouldn't feel worth it. So in the whole year, those three and a half months were the only paid work I really did. I also fully understand that being able to say "it's not worth it" is a luxury for some people. That's why I really recommend saving a bit more while you're still in Taiwan (not a lot, just a bit), so you can spend a month or two in Japan trying other ways of living, instead of only working. Outside the hotel job, I spent most of my time on "work exchange": working for a place to stay, with no pay. What it looked like in practice: 7 work exchanges in total: 4 stays of a month, 1 of three weeks, and 2 of a week Around 22 working hours a week on average, but about 40% of that felt more like play or experience, so it felt like about 12 hours a week I think a month is just the right length. You don't have to leave before you've gotten close (spending the time thinking "we're parting soon anyway" and not bothering to get to know each other), and it's long enough to build a relationship you'll keep in touch through. My paid job averaged 26 hours a week, so compared with that, 22 hours a week of work exchange is about the same but with no pay, which might feel unbalanced. All I can say is: "what you earn is the experience." I found most of my work exchanges through HelpX. The upside is the low membership fee (about 20 euros for two years). The downside is fewer options, so it suits people who aren't set on going to any particular place. Similar platforms like Workaway, which has the most users worldwide, have more choices but cost more. The room at one of my work exchanges When I found out my application went through and started planning, I kept asking myself: "What do I want to get out of this trip?" My answer was: experience all kinds of things I'd never experienced. I like cooking and trying ingredients, and I tried several kinds of grapes, strawberries and sweet potatoes, had dinners where everyone made one dish, and cooked Taiwanese food to share. I visited Japanese people's homes, and even lived in some. I feel you can see the "real Japanese people" best in ordinary daily life. I also talked with them about WWII history and business models, and asked things like "Japanese people don't actually like Taiwan, do they?" Besides Japanese people, I got to talk, travel and explore Japan with foreign friends from countries I'd never been to, or never even thought of going to. Those were my biggest gains. What if my Japanese isn't good enough? I left with Japanese at about N4 level, or a bit below, and over the year, the moments I regretted not being better at the language weren't as many as I'd imagined. Work exchange environments are usually more forgiving about language. Most hosts are used to being around foreigners, so broken Japanese (plus broken English) still gets the message across. Paid jobs demand better language skills, but there are lots of foreign workers in Japan and hiring working-holiday people is common, so quite a few jobs don't need Japanese. The work and choices are naturally more limited (usually cleaning, food prep, farm work), so it depends on what you're willing to do. Simple Japanese and a translation app cover most of daily life. I used the translation app a lot for paperwork and seeing doctors, and only rarely for chatting. Not because I understood everything, but because chatting through a translation app is honestly hard and awkward. You'll also meet people you can't really chat with, who still treat you kindly. There were moments of "I wish my Japanese were a bit better", when I'd get back to my room after a conversation and just couldn't swallow it (?), so I'd ask AI how to say something. That kind of thing kept me learning. After a year, my grammar is probably still N4, but my vocabulary grew a lot, my listening got very good (I can hear everything, though understanding it is another matter), speaking became a habit and I'm not scared to speak even in simple grammar, and my handwriting became terrible. Anyway, if you're not confident in your Japanese, don't worry. Once you're in Japan you'll have to speak, and you'll just practice little by little. Luggage: how to live out of one backpack My luggage was a 60-liter hiking backpack. I went back to Taiwan once before winter and added a carry-on suitcase after that. Later I met people with 3 to 5 pieces of luggage, which opened my eyes. My daily life in Taiwan is pretty minimal, so I never felt life was especially inconvenient. Looking back, "one bag all the way" totally works. A few things I learned: Make a packing list and weigh each item. You'll know the exact weight, and when you have to cut something, you can rank and compare items on the list and decide fast. It also works as a checklist before you leave. "Keep the load within a third of your body weight" was advice from a hiking friend. I weigh about 58 kg, so a third is around 19 kg, but my real comfortable limit was about 16 kg. I could walk with it fine, but lifting it up from a chair or the ground was harder. The most comfortable weight was about 13 kg. Bring 2 to 3 months' worth of consumables. The point is to give yourself time to research and buy local products at your own pace, though it depends on how often you move and your own habits. Dress in layers, onion style. Similar clothes can handle the temperature range from summer to autumn. I also recommend wool, which resists bacteria and odor, and technical hiking clothes: some are light, quick-drying, and look good too! Small gifts are a useful way to say thanks and to introduce Taiwan. I brought coffee beans and Taiwanese tea. Food goes over well with everyone, and Taiwanese tea in particular is something with real local character. You can brew it for everyone, and it becomes a topic of conversation. My packing list Why a backpack, and how I used it Choosing a backpack or a suitcase is purely personal. I like being able to move freely, and when I'm in a hurry I can run up the stairs (?). I especially didn't want to drag a big suitcase onto trains and buses and get in other people's way. Later in the trip, when the things I'd take back to Taiwan started to pile up, I switched to a lightweight duffel bag, fixed on top of the carry-on suitcase and pulled along together, so the backpack wouldn't get too heavy. When checking in for a flight, I packed the backpack into an IKEA FRAKTA bag (about 76 liters) at the airport, then stuffed the duffel bag full. That holds more weight than a suitcase of the same volume. I checked in a bit over 18 kg on the way home, and the backpack and the IKEA bag together weighed less than 1.5 kg. Checking the backpack in inside an IKEA FRAKTA bag My cooking gear I cooked for myself about 90% of the time. For gear, I bought a 16 cm stainless steel saucepan (about 400 g) and carried it around. The pots at work exchanges or shared kitchens are often in bad shape, and I'm not a fan of Teflon nonstick pans. This size is plenty for noodle soup, stir-fries and pancakes. The downside is that fried eggs are harder to get right. I also carried a food pouch (Pockeat, a product from good day agooday). It's handy for taking fruit with me when I go out, or cooking leftover ingredients and taking them along. Reusable lunch boxes depend on the place, since some places have few bowls and plates, or aren't suited for hogging them. I personally recommend eggs and salted kelp, which get along with any other ingredient. Learning to use the microwave makes cooking a lot easier. Also, physical work really does make you need sugary drinks, and even people who never drink bubble tea in Taiwan give in... Breakfast one day Dinner one day Paperwork, and some advice For things like the residence card, national pension and a post office account, I recommend finding a place where you can stay for 2 to 3 months after you arrive in Japan and getting everything done you can. A lot of documents take business days to be mailed, up to a month at most, and if your schedule gets fragmented later, it becomes very painful to sort out. I didn't apply for a My Number Card, but from other people's experience, with the card some procedures can be done directly online, saving trips to city hall or the time it takes to mail things. If you've just arrived in Japan and still have time to stay put, consider getting one too. It'll make enrolling in things, filing taxes and other procedures a lot easier later. As for national health insurance, I only found out I had to enroll when I was about to start paid work, when the agency helping me reminded me. But both times I handled my address registration at city hall, I was asked "Do you need to enroll in insurance?", as if it were optional. In fact enrolling in national health insurance is an obligation! (*You don't need to enroll only if your workplace provides "social insurance".) If you plan to move around a lot and most of your time isn't paid work, you can consider travel accident and illness insurance. But note that its limit is usually 180 days, and it doesn't cover work accidents, so be sure to check with your insurance broker whether it suits your plans. I actually did make a claim once. I went to a clinic for a rash from insect bites, and because I had no national health insurance I paid the full amount (about 4,000 to 5,000 yen). Afterwards, following my broker's instructions, I made my own medical certificate, had the doctor fill it in and stamp it, and applied for reimbursement after I got back to Taiwan. So how much did it all cost? (for reference only) The actual spending was about NT$264,000 (11 months only, not counting the almost one month I spent back in Taiwan). By category: Food 42% Accommodation 17% Entertainment 16% (souvenirs, tickets, hot springs and other non-essentials) Transport 15% Daily life 9% (necessities and medical) Insurance 2% Pie chart of working holiday spending in Japan by category These numbers vary a lot from person to person, but at least they can serve as a reference. About 1,010 working hours in total (paid work plus work exchange) About 60 days of overnight trips, and at least 25 day trips Finally "Am I building up things that give me choices?" A while ago, while I was gathering material for this post, I read this line in Joe Chang's Facebook post, and suddenly felt it was very close to the plans and choices I made this year. I'm no longer a 20-something with plenty of time to try and fail, and on this trip I knew I had to gain something besides new experiences. Even though I still can't clearly say what exactly all these things I encountered are adding up to, in some odd moments these gains really did become chances to talk with others and to deepen relationships. Having felt this again and again, I'm convinced that this learning, this curiosity, all this knowledge and experience that can't be turned into money or built into expertise, is meaningful. To end with an old saying: many times, "every arrangement is the best arrangement."

title: Chicken House Notes | Glad I'm Not a Farm Animal
abstract: As the days go by and the size gap widens, the ones who can't keep up may get pushed away from water and feed, and the gap only grows.
text: I recently started working in a chicken house. When people hear "chicken house", they probably think of egg-laying hens, and then the cage debate. But the house I work in raises broilers, the kind of chicken you picture when you think of fried chicken. A batch is normally raised for 35 days and reaches around 2 kg. They grow that fast because of breeding, not because of growth hormones (that's a false rumor, honestly no hormones). Still, because they grow so fast, there's real animal-welfare talk about their skeletons not being able to hold up all that meat (and that part is true). The house is floor-raised: one flat surface, no perches, no cages, covered with a thick layer of rice husks (I think wood shavings work too). It's a closed environment, cooled with fans, water curtains and misting, and warmed with heaters. The first week is when most of them die. Infections. Eyes that never opened, so they can't find water or feed by themselves. Chicks with no energy, who can barely take two steps even when you nudge them. Lame legs that limit their movement. And even the ones who can still run and eat, but whose growth just can't keep up with the rest. At first they may look the same as everyone else, but as the days pass and the size gap widens, falling behind means getting pushed away from water and feed, which widens the gap even more. They also get bullied (the flock has a very clear hierarchy). On my rounds I pick up the ones who have died (sometimes I see other chickens walking right over them), watch for any odd behavior, and think: "Which kind would I be? Would I have been born with some defect? Would I be one who can't keep up on growth? Would I be culled at some point?" Jason Leung on Unsplash

title: Working at a Ski Resort Hotel: Life in Snow Country, Sugadaira Kogen, Nagano
tags: Nagano｜Ueda｜Sugadaira Kogen｜Resort Baito｜Life in Snow Country｜Snow Scenery｜Ski Resort｜Working Holiday
abstract: My one wish for the working holiday was to "spend a winter somewhere with snow." So from December 2025 to March 2026 I worked at a hotel in Sugadaira Kogen: shifts of breakfast, room cleaning and dinner, ordinary days at minus ten degrees, and the two other Taiwanese people I spent three and a half months with.
text: The year-long working holiday finally brought my first, and only, real job! I wanted to spend a winter where there's snow "Spend a winter somewhere with snow, and go somewhere I can learn to ski" was the only wish I had for the working holiday. My Japanese was limited (by job standards, honestly it was "can't speak Japanese"). I'd thought about Hokkaido for a while, but while an agent was contacting places for me, I found waiting for interviews and replies too stressful and too much hassle, so I just took whatever came (?). The hotel in Sugadaira Kogen The hotel is in Sugadaira Kogen in Nagano, at about 1,300 meters above sea level, an hour by bus from Ueda Station. Most visitors are Japanese. It's a ski destination in winter and a holy land for sports training camps in summer, with lots of sports grounds (all buried under snow in winter). The hotel can hold over three hundred people, and its main guests are school groups, so when it's busy, it's truly insane. There were nearly 20 winter-only workers like me, mostly Thai, then Indonesian, and Taiwanese people were the fewest, just the three of us. Apart from the odd little drama, everyone was pretty respectful, tolerant and friendly, and we even had a New Year's Eve dinner together. The Japan I saw from inside the hotel At work you can observe how different schools manage things and how they interact with students. One school's morning call came with a woman teacher's singing, and I saw a male teacher yelling and scolding a student until they cried, which was so interesting! There was also a boys' school group: buzz-cut, tough-looking high schoolers who didn't make a fuss while queuing in the crowded buffet line, and who very gentlemanly let the girl behind them go first when picking up their food. I was lucky to catch a small corner of Japanese culture from an angle I'd never had before. Shifts and daily rhythm It was shift work, roughly split into three slots: breakfast, room cleaning (plus lunch) and dinner. I started around 5 to 6 in the morning and finished around 8 to 9 at night, and sometimes napped in the afternoon after getting up so early. Even though I only worked 6 to 8 hours a day, I felt kind of foggy the whole time, and the rest of each day seemed to disappear if I so much as lazed around... I guess it had been so long since I'd done a regular nine-to-five that I forgot this feeling XD Restaurant vs. room cleaning I liked working in the restaurant better. It felt like playing a management game: restocking dishes, wiping down the buffet counter, clearing plates and so on. I liked room cleaning less, mainly because the cleaning standard was sooo far from my bare minimum. Doing this job also made me lose faith in humanity (hotel cleaning), and I keep complaining "wiping it makes it dirtier than not wiping" and "trust no one." Overall, like any job, fun and misery always come together, and you only know the flavor once you've tried it. Winter in snow country: how my body reacted Winter temperatures here ran from about −10 to 0 degrees, and it wasn't as cold as I'd imagined. At least if I put on all my clothes, I was mostly fine, and I hardly wore a beanie. Even though it didn't feel that cold, for the first month and a half my nose was always bloody, my scalp seemed to get dandruff from the dryness, the knuckles on the backs of my hands bled two or three times from dryness, my heels cracked for the first time in my life, and I caught a cold in my second week there. Other than that everything was fine, and I never even slipped on the snow! (That's worth being a bit proud of, right!!) The daily life snow brings Snow brought a completely different daily life. A 7-minute walk to work could turn into 15. The driveway in front of the dorm, with over 20 meters of piled-up snow, took several of us 30 minutes to shovel. The windowsill of my dorm room was a ready-made fridge; in cold weather the window frame iced over and the window wouldn't open, and in warmer weather I had to clean up a little lake of meltwater on the sill. I needed the heater on in the room to survive, but the electric heater has a safety feature that turns it off after 8 hours, and several times I forgot to turn it back on before bed and woke up shivering. And before I could ski, heavy snow was annoying, but once I could ski, I thought "please, more snow!" The many faces of snow, and icicles Snow comes in many forms. Fresh snow is soft and fluffy like cotton candy ice. After a day or two of good weather, the surface starts to melt and sparkle in the sun, and it sticks together easily, which is perfect for snowballs and snowmen. Melt a bit more and it becomes big, clear crystals like traditional shaved ice, and after that a smooth sheet of ice, which was my least favorite moment. I'd hop left and right, dodge left and right, looking for somewhere safer to step, and the walk to work took even longer. On days of steady melting, lots of icicles form under the eaves. Looking for a safe, low spot to harvest (?) big long icicles and sticking them outside my room window (?) was my daily fun. I once saw a guest harvest a huge icicle (and they even pointed out where they'd harvested it), which shows harvesting icicles isn't weird! I'm not alone! XD My fellow Taiwanese in the dorm: Pin Deep in the mountains, far away from everything, it feels inevitable that workers from different countries in the dorm would mix with locals, and get really close. Pin was my roommate, and this was the first stop of her working holiday. Like Doraemon, she'd brought lots of daily supplies and Taiwanese snacks and kept up the quality of life, and she saved me, who hadn't brought a hair dryer or a single hanger. Our personalities are very different but we clicked right away. We're both from Taiwan, we both like cooking, and living in the same room, working together, venting to each other and picking up trash to reuse (?) helped us get along. Ryu, who showed up a few weeks later The other Taiwanese person, Ryu, showed up a few weeks later. He's a guy who hasn't been poisoned by society yet and is making the most of his youth on a working holiday. Maybe because he has an older sister and a younger sister at home, he's very comfortable to be around, though now and then he acts like a boy (brat) and makes you want to roll your eyes. (He also became a professional icicle harvester later on XD) What made us close was, I think, chatting during a break and finding out he had a rice cooker, then finding out he could ski, so on days off we ate together, skied and went on trips. On boring days, Pin and I would barge into Ryu's big single room to find something fun to do. (Not only was the room bigger, the lights were even brighter!) Precious and lovely time It was a precious and lovely time. Three and a half months is not short, and the three of us Taiwanese, who had no choice but to make friends with whoever was in front of us, got along really well. We worked hard and earned money, and played hard too. Life was simple and ordinary and happiness came easily, which felt a little naive. I'm grateful that I still get to be so naive. Further reading: 〈A Working Holiday Year in Japan: Preparation, Costs, and a Life That Isn't Mostly Working〉 (2026-08-31)

title: A Side Quest from Work Exchange: Cooking with Japanese People, for Japanese People
abstract: The staff member at "Machimachi Information Center," Shiho-san, who makes tofu for a living, invited me to help prepare their monthly lunch diner, so I made braised pork rice, sesame oil chicken soup and douhua for Japanese guests.
text: I went back to the community café at Mineyama Station, "まちまち案内所 (Machimachi Information Center)" (I wrote about my first visit in the previous post, 〈A Day Trip in Kyotango: Kumihama, Amino and Mineyama〉), for a second time. Side quest: invited to cook at a lunch diner A few days later I came back to Machimachi for the second time and met the owner (whose Chinese is amazing) and the man in charge of planning the "一箱本棚オーナー制度" (a shared bookshelf where each person owns one box). We chatted a lot in my broken Japanese and Chinese. One of the staff invited me to her workshop to make a lunch diner together: braised pork rice, chicken soup, pickled tomatoes and other Taiwanese-style dishes. It was like triggering a side quest. Besides my work exchange in Kumihama, I got to run a restaurant for the first time, and it was very memorable. This staff member is Shiho-san, who makes tofu for a living, and her workshop is in Iyo. Shiho-san loves Taiwanese food and knows the common ingredients (for Japanese people the signature Taiwanese flavors seem to be star anise / five-spice powder and fried shallots). She's happy to try all kinds of methods, and she's very good at adding or swapping ingredients, making creative but tasty dishes on a traditional base. The lunch diner is hosted by Shiho-san once a month, and usually a few older ladies help with prep and serve out front. This time I helped with recipe suggestions and prep. What we made Braised pork rice: We used astringent persimmon (Mino persimmon) in place of sugar. I've kind of forgotten, but I think the pork was hand-cut. The braised eggs were a last-minute addition and probably didn't soak up much flavor, but at least the pork was braised the night before! Shiho-san added pickled vegetables and fresh greens on top. Sesame oil chicken soup: I used a good amount of sesame oil, but in the end the sesame flavor was very mild. We later added daikon, tofu, jujubes, and a few leaves for decoration. Pickled tomatoes: Nothing special XD Douhua: We used softer nigari tofu to make douhua, and it was really very close to the real thing (I think it could sell in Taiwan). It wasn't the classic peanut version, but red beans are the easiest and a very common topping! (It was peanut season then, but maybe peanuts in Japan are expensive? Shiho-san mentioned that if she ever gets the chance to visit Taiwan, she'd like to try Taiwanese peanuts.) On Japanese side dishes and taste Japanese people don't like or aren't used to eating one flavor all the way through. There always has to be something else to go with it. For example, the braised pork rice got some leafy greens on top. We're used to having greens on the side too, but Taiwan and Japan seem to understand the side dish a little differently. Ours is a dish with its own proper name, like braised napa cabbage or braised bamboo shoots, while theirs seems more decorative, mainly there to change up the texture. The pickled tomatoes are also a small "箸休め" (chopstick rest) dish, meant to reset your palate after a heavily flavored main, and they seemed to have an even lower status than a side dish (?). They also don't seem to like very strong, stimulating flavors. For example, the braised pork was made runnier, and it can't be the thick, oily, salty or sweet kind that goes with rice. And sesame oil chicken soup made entirely with rice wine, still with a bit of the alcohol flavor, and with a layer of oil floating on top, is probably hard to get used to. Afterwards Later, in May 2026, I did a work exchange with Shiho-san, which became the last work-exchange stay of my working holiday. Further reading: 〈A Day Trip in Kyotango: Kumihama, Amino and Mineyama〉

title: A Day Trip in Kyotango: Kumihama, Amino and Mineyama
tags: Kyoto｜Kyotango｜Kumihama｜Amino｜Mineyama｜Kotohikihama Beach｜Singing Sand｜Inaba Residence｜Nyoiji Temple｜Kotohira Shrine｜Komaineko｜Foot Bath｜Neapolitan Pizza｜Fujiwara Sengyoten uRashiMa
abstract: A wealthy merchant's mansion and Nyoiji Temple in Kumihama, Neapolitan pizza in Amino, the singing sands of Kotohikihama and a seaside foot bath, and a community café in Mineyama plus Japan's only "komaineko" cat guardian statue.
text: Notes from a full-day or half-day trip around Kyotango, split into three areas by station. Kumihama Station: the Inaba merchant residence and Nyoiji Temple I was staying on the narrow sandbar of Kumihama Bay, and the nearest supermarket was in the station area on the opposite shore, directly to the south. Spot one is the "Inaba residence, home of a wealthy merchant", which is just a rich family's house: not super special, but not boring either. Two exhibits stuck with me. One was a bridal palanquin (嫁入り籠) you can sit in. It's super tiny and narrow, and you can only hug your knees or kneel, and even if Japanese women back then were only 140 to 145 cm tall, this was still the only way to sit! The other was a Japanese koto you can play freely, the first time I'd seen one like that!! Spot two is Nyoiji Temple. The plants and trees are well kept and it's very calming, and when you leave, the gate faces Kumihama Bay, beautiful right to the last moment. Amino Station I set out in the morning, took the train to Amino Station, and walked 40 to 50 minutes to Fujiwara Sengyoten uRashiMa for pizza as lunch, then walked another hour to Kotohikihama. Fujiwara Sengyoten uRashiMa I went alone to this pizza place in Amino, "Fujiwara Sengyoten uRashiMa". In 2012 the owner won a silver medal in the Fantasia (creative) category at the Neapolitan Pizza Olympics (Pizza Olympic). The shop is small, with about 5 to 6 seats. Someone had a reservation that day, but I got lucky and got the one remaining seat. There are lots of pizza options: besides the classic flavors, there are original pizzas using local ingredients and seafood, and you can order half-and-half, so even one person can have two flavors, which is great! The appetizer platter was rich, and I think each was drizzled with olive oil or something before serving (I forgot). Each had a different flavor, but several had the same oily texture, which felt a bit... distracting? One appetizer that particularly stuck with me was fried sweet potato bits with a sugar coating, very much like the "Yongbo sweet potato crisps" you can buy at Taiwanese supermarkets. (I later brought some of those crisps for Japanese people to try, and it was a sweet potato snack texture they'd never had either.) Overall, it wasn't super, super amazing, but it was definitely tasty, and not that traditional or predictable. They all had a sense of variation, and I recommend it! I spent around 5,000 yen eating alone (pizza + appetizer platter + a soft drink), which hurt a bit... hahaha Notes Fujiwara Sengyoten uRashiMa: 11:30 to 19:00, closed Thursdays (other days off are on their IG). Pizza is around 2,500 yen. 40 minutes on foot from Amino Station, or 4 minutes by bus plus 20 minutes on foot... Kotohikihama Kotohikihama, the singing beach, is a famous nationally designated natural monument and scenic spot. The wife of the strawberry farm owner mentioned it when she heard I was coming to Kyotango next. It must be pretty famous, right? So why were there only two or three visitors...? From uRashiMa I walked an hour to the beach (not recommended, so tiring XD). On the way I took a break at an ice cream shop run at a ranch (the ice cream was so-so... my top recommendation in Kyotango is "Sora", which also started as a ranch and is the most famous). The wind on the beach was huge, sand flying everywhere, hardly anyone around, a bit scary. When I stopped and listened carefully, I really could hear the sand clinking and rustling, apparently because the sand is 75% quartz and makes a sound when rubbed. And you can really feel the sand hitting your body and your camera lens. When I looked it up, I found there's also an area near the same spot called "Taikohama" (Drum Beach), where stamping hard supposedly resonates with the bedrock and makes a "don don" sound like a drum. (I didn't know then so I didn't go, so all I can say is "supposedly".) On Google Maps I found a foot bath (Open-Air-Bath) landmark, roughly below the campground, next to the wooden stairs. It's a concrete artificial pool of about one tsubo. It looks very basic and nothing special, but soaking your feet while looking at the sea is what makes it special! You get the achievement of "soaking while looking at the sea". So cool. When I arrived, three middle-aged foreigners who live in Japan were soaking their feet, and they said only locals know about this foot bath. On the way back to the bus stop I picked persimmons from the roadside, then took a bus of about 15 minutes back to Amino Station. So fast, haha! Notes About 15 minutes by bus from Amino Station, then a 10-minute walk. Not open in winter. In July and August you can soak in a swimsuit, and in spring and autumn only the foot bath is open. Mineyama Station: community café, Kotohira Shrine and the komaineko Mineyama is where daily-life conveniences are most concentrated in Kyotango. I went in the early afternoon, first to "まちまち案内所 (Machimachi Information Center)", a place like a community café where people come to exchange ideas. It's a big space that used to be a lumber shop. I was mainly interested in the model of the citizen-started "みんなの図書館 (everyone's library)", since each shop plans and runs it differently, so whenever I have time I visit different examples. After looking around, I originally wanted to go to the regional revitalization hub "Roots (Kyotango City Future Challenge Exchange Center)", but a big part of that space serves high school students, so I loitered in front of it three times and never dared to go in...! (So regretful! I came back half a year later and still didn't go QQ) Next I went to Kotohira Shrine, ate takoyaki nearby, and went to see Japan's only "komaineko" (cat guardian) stone statue. In the end I decided to go back to Machimachi for an early dinner before leaving, and started chatting with the staff member serving me. We talked a lot about cooking, about how I didn't dare go into Roots, and about the shop's "一箱本棚オーナー制度" (one-box bookshelf owner system) and so on. She told me the person who planned the system would come by some day. A few days later I went a second time, and something unexpected happened, which I wrote about in another post: 〈A Side Quest from Work Exchange: Cooking with Japanese People, for Japanese People〉. Further reading: 〈A Working Holiday Year in Japan: Preparation, Costs, and a Life That Isn't Mostly Working〉 (2026-08-31)

title: Local Produce in Kyotango, and Matsuba Crab Season Is Open!
tags: Kyoto｜Kyotango｜Kumihama｜Matsuba Crab｜Seiko Crab｜Benimaiko Sweet Potato｜Shinko Pear｜Oshu Pear｜Atago Pear｜Kumihama
abstract: I biked around looking for unstaffed farm stands and found sweet potatoes, pears, fresh peanuts and giant shiitake. I went to the ranch Sora for ice cream twice, and of course there was the matsuba crab I couldn't miss!
text: During my three weeks in Kumihama in November, three or four days had nothing planned except biking around aimlessly: looking for unstaffed farm stands, going to the famous tourist ranch Sora for ice cream (I liked it so much I went twice), eating all the seasonal specialties (peanuts, sweet potatoes, pears, matsuba crab), and enjoying the autumn scenery, sunrises and sunsets of a fishing village in the countryside. This is the most ordinary part of my stay there, and still worth writing down. Farm stands: cheap, fresh, and with ingredients you rarely see in supermarkets There are lots of farm stands, big and small, around Kumihama. They're cheap and fresh, and they have ingredients you rarely see in supermarkets, like fresh peanuts (just boil them and they're delicious!), giant shiitake (3 huge ones for 500 yen, very thick and meaty, amazing fried!), green bitter melon and so on. I also ate the seasonal matsuba crab, sweet potatoes and pears. If I get another chance, I'd like to come back in mid to late August for the famous melons, Nijisseiki pears, plus peaches and grapes~ (There are still grapes in November too, but I'd eaten so many in Himeji that I think I only bought one bunch here.) Matsuba crab Crab fishing opens in November, so eat it up while you're young and gout is probably not a problem yet! Only the males are called matsuba crab, and each one comes with a little origin ID tag (colors differ by region). Prices range from 2,000 to 15,000 yen each, and you can get one with a few legs missing for a reasonable price of under 6,000 yen. Females are small, usually called kobako crab or seiko crab, at around 600 to 800 yen each. Boiled is the common way. I paid 5,000 yen for one at Shibayama Port but found it not sweet enough. My host said boiling washes out the sweetness, so I bought another one for 3,000 yen and steamed it myself. It was a bit better but I still felt it wasn't enough (though it was already really good!). Then, back in Taiwan at the end of the year, at a work celebration dinner I had all-you-can-eat matsuba crab and found it super sweet (???)... maybe it's because someone else was paying?! I also tried crab leg sashimi, and didn't fall in love with it. I still prefer the rich crab flavor when it's cooked~ Sweet potato: Benimaiko grown on sand dunes Kyotango sweet potatoes get their character from being grown on sand dunes, which helps root crops build up starch and sugar. Autumn and winter are the season, and lots of farm stands sell them. I bought two kinds for a simple comparison: one was the most common variety at the time (I forgot which), and the other was Kyotango's "Benimaiko", a chestnut-type sweet potato. After roasting in the oven, just looking at the cross-section, you can tell Benimaiko is super fluffy with little fiber, and it really does taste like chestnut. Pears: Shinko, Oshu, Atago Pears are also an important crop of this region, and November is the late harvest. The three I ate, "Shinko, Oshu and Atago", were all huge, mostly the gift-giving type. I thought they tasted about as good as in Taiwan (comparing with Taiwan's Baodao Ganlu pear), and the price was about 80% of Taiwan's, or about the same. I don't remember the weights of the big and small ones, but the price was between 400 and 1,000 yen each. (Note: "Baodao Ganlu pear" is a Taiwanese variety that Japan doesn't have.) I'm not eloquent enough to taste the difference between "Shinko" and "Oshu", but they were broadly close to the Ganlu pear, the kind that's thrillingly sweet, showy and generous, like a big-hearted person (though Ganlu is sweet to the point of hurting your teeth). The info says Oshu is a dreamy premium item! The other, "Atago", turned out to be billed as "Japan's biggest pear" when I looked it up, and it tasted noticeably different. It's not as sweet or soft, but it's dense and a bit firmer, like a person with real depth and a mellow personality. I bought this one at Kusakabe Farm. (Eating too many pears gives you diarrhea, so watch out.) Further reading: 〈A Working Holiday Year in Japan: Preparation, Costs, and a Life That Isn't Mostly Working〉 (2026-08-31)

title: Work Exchange: An Oyster Fishing Village on Kumihama Bay, Kyotango
tags: Kyoto｜Kyotango｜Kumihama Bay｜Kumihama Oyster｜Oyster Farm｜Work Exchange｜Working Holiday｜Single Seed Oyster
abstract: My third work exchange was at an oyster farmer's home on Kumihama Bay, at the northernmost tip of Kyoto facing the Sea of Japan. I stayed three weeks and got a taste of unfamiliar work on the water.
text: My third work exchange was in Kyoto Prefecture... at the northernmost point, facing the Sea of Japan! It was the second most remote place I've done a work exchange (though at the time it was the number one). The house is 3 km from the nearest station (Kotenbashi Station on the Tango Railway) and 6 km from a convenience store or supermarket. It's remote, but I didn't find it that inconvenient: the host would drive us to the supermarket for shopping, and I was pretty carefree with a bicycle. Living at an oyster farmer's home: host Atsushi-san I stayed here for three weeks. Host Atsushi-san is a third-generation oyster farmer on Kumihama Bay, and you step out of the back door of the house and you're at the sea. Every house has its own pier for a work boat, and the oyster rafts sit in the middle of a lagoon, five minutes away by boat. He also runs a two-story guesthouse with three rooms in total, which his grandmother started. There are quite a few family-run guesthouses like this in the area, and the guests are mostly Japanese people who come in autumn and winter for the matsuba crab, whose season has just opened, and for Kumihama Bay oysters. Atsushi-san speaks very good English, so during my stay one or two groups of foreign guests stayed too. Work with no fixed content Work here started at 9 every day and ended before noon, with no fixed content, and often I only found out what the day's job was once I got there. For example: making sandbags and pushing them into the sea as boat anchors, organizing the boxes of bird clams (torigai) on the oyster rafts, sorting oyster babies, guesthouse cleaning, making beds and serving meals (I was even surprised with a tip of a 1,000-yen note wrapped in tissue paper, and apparently tipping servers used to be quite common in the old days), tidying the storage room, the kitchen fridge, and so on. The work was varied and mostly easy, and I could do it at my own pace. Even organizing the kitchen was something that I and the other work exchange guest, Samuel from France (he's a baker, and we had lots of opinions about the state of the kitchen XD), suggested doing. It didn't feel like work here. It felt much more like really being on holiday in a seaside fishing village, and going on an overnight trip was totally fine too. The short hours are a key factor, but a lot of the credit goes to Atsushi-san. He's a gentle person, never stingy about responding to what we needed, works almost alongside us, and treated us like friends. Oyster and Tango torigai farming on Kumihama Bay Kumihama Bay is a lagoon on the Sea of Japan coast, and its "oyster farming landscape" was designated a Kyoto Prefecture cultural landscape. The main oyster farming method is to drill holes in scallop shells with lots of baby oysters attached, fix them at intervals on a rope, and hang them vertically under the water from a raft, where they feed on plankton. My host's family uses a newer method, "single seed basket farming". Each baby oyster is separate, and they're put together into a roomy, mansion-like net basket and hung in the sea. They don't crowd each other's growing space, and when the waves knock them together, the growth rings on their edges get worn off, so the shell thickens in a concentrated way and can form a deep cup inside. The yield is relatively low, but the size is uniform and the shape is beautiful, and it's made only for the top-end raw market. What I got to experience was this: the oyster babies, only three weeks old and recently bought, come in big and small sizes, and I helped separate them by size so the big ones don't take the food and starve the small ones. Generally, oysters start being raised in spring and are harvested in winter. The reason they started in November here is that the water is colder then and harmful fouling organisms have almost stopped reproducing, so the oysters survive better. Growth is slower in winter, but growing up in the cold and the wind and waves builds a strong body! The rafts used for oysters here also raise "Tango torigai" (Tango bird clams), of which there are very few similar species in Taiwan, and the info says it's Japan's top-grade bird clam brand. They're also sunk into the sea by hanging, but loaded a bit differently: in basket-like containers with sand they can burrow into, and the opening is fitted with a grill-like net cover to keep out predators, while the tasty plankton still gets in~ (The summer of 2025 was so hot that the Tango torigai in Kumihama Bay were wiped out entirely 🥲) Biking around aimlessly Here, biking around aimlessly was what I did most. I loved looking for unstaffed farm stands, tasting local produce, and enjoying the autumn scenery, sunrises and sunsets of a fishing village in the countryside. For farther trips, I biked 50 minutes to Kumihama Station, or took the train to nearby Toyooka, Amino and Mineyama, and I also went to Kinosaki Onsen and Amanohashidate, one of Japan's Three Views. None of these places is more than a 30-minute drive away, and most aren't famous sights, but I really like spending a day or an afternoon picking a few little-known landmarks or restaurants I want to eat at as destinations, then enjoying the surprise detours and unexpected views along the way. The bike ride I remember most The image that stayed with me most in Kyotango was one bike ride. First I rode along a slightly winding concrete path with fruit trees on both sides. Then the same path turned from concrete to grass, with two bare tracks worn by cars, and my bike wheels reluctantly pushed on across the bumpy grass. In the distance was no longer an orchard but a small stretch of woods. The woods section was short and I could see the sky at the exit, so I wasn't scared at all (okay, maybe 10% scared). But after less than twenty meters, a steep uphill appeared that my 3-speed city bike couldn't conquer, and after I got off and pushed for five or six meters, I saw a super long downhill that made me cheer (and on smooth concrete, too). I happily coasted down, enjoying the suddenly open view and the wind on my face. Then on my right appeared at least 30 little Jizo statues in tiny red caps and bibs, lined up like a choir, with neat rows of gravestones stretching out on both sides. "Eh? Eh?" I didn't know whether I should brake. Speeding along so happily felt kind of disrespectful, so I ended up squeezing and releasing the brakes guiltily. At the bottom of the slope was a big paved farm road, and the farm stand was diagonally across, back to reality (?). In just a few minutes I felt a complicated change of feelings, truly unforgettable. Thank you for all the care and the conversations! Further reading: 〈A Working Holiday Year in Japan: Preparation, Costs, and a Life That Isn't Mostly Working〉 (2026-08-31)

title: Work Exchange: A Strawberry Farm near Himeji, and No Strawberries in October
abstract: My second work exchange was a month at a strawberry-picking farm in Himeji: early mornings, quiet me-time greenhouse work, and a host and a farm family who took really good care of me.
text: A real work exchange, my second one! This month I did a work exchange at a strawberry-picking farm in Himeji (the kind where you pick your own!). It's only 25 minutes by car from Himeji Station, the most urban place I've done a work exchange, and yet I ran into a deer by the road next to the farm...! Apartment-style dorm The housing was a 2LDK apartment, fully Western style, two people per room, so up to 4 people in total. The soundproofing, on the other hand, was fully Japanese style haha. I remember once bothering a roommate who was sleeping in the room while I was using my computer in the living room. For about half a month of my stay, 3 to 4 people lived there. I came here with my social energy drained, and I honestly didn't even have the energy for awkward small talk, so I didn't make particular friends with the other work-exchange people. Only in the first week did I chat a bit more with my Chinese roommate. About the work I worked 5 days a week, 5 hours a day (07:00 to 12:00), which meant getting up at 6. That wasn't easy to get used to for a long-time night owl like me, but the work was fairly static and quiet, and I slowly woke up while working, so it didn't feel especially hard or painful. It's a tiny self-observation, but I liked the feeling of getting to know myself a little bit more. The work was in a greenhouse. October temperatures were a bit hot but never unbearable, and later, when autumn came and the temperature swings grew, the lowest when I left in the morning was only 7 degrees, and I found the greenhouse warmer, which was great. From my childhood memories of strawberry picking, strawberries were mostly grown on the ground, and this was the first time I saw raised-bed strawberries. The cost is higher and there's more work, but workers can stand while working, which I have to say is pretty friendly. The main jobs were removing old leaves, pulling weeds and removing runners, and besides that I fixed plastic sheeting, transplanted, swept, washed and stored seedling containers, reinforced the cloth tents, and so on. Besides us work-exchange people, the farm had about 7 regular employees (not all full-time, some were contract workers with different working days), with some older (50 to 60?) and some young (from 20). People didn't chat much on breaks, and rarely while working (it's not that chatting is forbidden, you'd still occasionally hear the older employees chatting), and overall the atmosphere was quiet with no social pressure. I didn't talk much with the regular staff (limited Japanese was a big reason), but in the small interactions during work, I could still feel their friendliness. I also really liked how breaks were institutionalized and happened on time: a 30-minute break at exactly 9, and if the weather was too hot, another water break of about 15 minutes at 11. There was none of "someone deliberately shows off by doing more, which puts pressure on everyone else", and the boss never squeezed extra hours out of us. (Taiwanese office-worker trauma, and here I got the respect of "being treated like a person".) I loved this time, probably because I really needed to stop for a while. With my hands doing repetitive labor, I could talk to myself, think about what I'd experienced and what I'd taken from it, and even stop to take notes on my phone. When there was nothing to think about, I'd just let my mind go blank or listen to podcasts. That's good for someone like me whose brain never stops and who isn't used to zoning out, and the labor still produced results. The yuzu orchard, snakes, and host Leon Besides the strawberry farm, I also helped once or twice at host Leon's yuzu orchard. The yuzu trees grow on a slope, which isn't easy to move around on, and the main jobs were weeding and removing spiderwebs, which fits my image of hard farm labor better (hey). I also learned for the first time that yuzu branches have hard thorns like roses, which is a bit at odds with my image of sweet yuzu wine (?). When we went out for lunch, I saw a snake sunbathing by the orchard road, and when we came back after eating it was still in the same spot! So relaxed! Japanese yuzu (ゆず) is different from what Taiwanese people call "pomelo" (柚子). It's absolutely not something you peel and eat raw. If you're looking for the Taiwanese kind of pomelo in Japan, look for "buntan" (ぶんたん). Also, I ate lots of mandarin oranges in autumn and winter, and some varieties are actually more like what we think of as pomelo, and the white pith is bitter and can't be eaten~~ Outside of work, Leon usually lives in the same apartment building as the work-exchange people, and his role is a bit like our babysitter haha! He's the school-bus driver who takes us to work and back, and he also prepares ingredients for us. You can chat with him about whatever you want to know, from farming knowledge to personal experiences (Leon isn't Japanese), and he invites us to meals and events and shares all kinds of information. I was lucky to ride in his cool Land Rover Defender in the last few days, the coolest car I've ever ridden in! Visibly cool! The Fukuda family The farm owner, the Fukuda family, was also very friendly! Fukuda-san's wife came to the farm to let us try matcha, took us for a walk by the sea, to a festival, and out for taiyaki. Later, for a while I was the only work-exchange person left, and I went to their home for dinner, to a market, to other festivals and so on, leaving great memories. I went to the following two festivals with the Fukuda family: 10/19 Tomishima Shrine, autumn festival: a local festival in Tatsuno City, with five districts taking part and different age groups working together. It started with a children's mikoshi (portable shrine), which was very cute. The info says there's a lion dance, but I left before seeing it~ 11/2 Aioi Tenman Shrine, autumn festival: a local festival in Aioi City, where each town has pairs taking turns dancing different steps in the "shishimai" (lion dance), and children take turns playing the music. Children who aren't performing stay on the stage, and some kids waited until they dozed off, so adults would come up from below and nudge them on the back, super cute! The Japanese people talked to me about Taiwan's lion dance, and they think Taiwanese lions are very cute XD Revisiting in late November: DIY okonomiyaki At the end of November I went back to Himeji for two days. Besides going back to the farm to see and eat strawberries, Fukuda-san took me to a place where you can make your own okonomiyaki! It started when we had a meal with the Fukudas and they took me to the well-known Himeji teppanyaki chain "喃風", where a big iron griddle took up most of the table. I mentioned DIY okonomiyaki and learned that this type of place isn't actually common. Later they specially took me to a restaurant where you can really make your own okonomiyaki. I'm so grateful~~ I also had dinner with the family, and we went to a popular café that makes desserts with the farm's strawberries. On the night I left, they even walked me to the station to see me off, which really moved me~~~ (For privacy I won't mention anyone else's names, but the whole family's names are all related to good weather, which I love, so cute XD) Notes I found out later that the place we ate at was "Komehachi (米八)", an established okonomiyaki restaurant of nearly 40 years, in Aboshi, Himeji. "喃風": a teppanyaki chain that started in Himeji, famous for its original dish "doroyaki", which is soft and mushy, and after cutting a piece you dip it in broth before eating. A very special dish! October, when so many people looked after me, was full of gratitude! Further reading: 〈A Working Holiday Year in Japan: Preparation, Costs, and a Life That Isn't Mostly Working〉 (2026-08-31)

title: Himeji in October: The Fighting Festival, Moon Viewing and Seasonal Produce
abstract: What's on in Himeji in October? Besides the classics, the national-treasure Himeji Castle and the thousand-year-old temple Engyoji on Mount Shosha, there's the shocking Nada no Kenka Matsuri, the mid-autumn moon viewing, and a national pottery fair. Plus I ate my fill of the Seto Inland Sea's seasonal catch, a bumper crop of grapes, and persimmons picked by the roadside.
text: In autumn 2025, I did a work exchange for a month at a strawberry-picking farm on the outskirts of Himeji. Besides visiting the two classic spots, Himeji Castle and Engyoji Temple, I went to festivals big and small (autumn really is festivals everywhere!) and ate my fill of seasonal seafood and fruit. Himeji Castle: the largest and most structurally complex surviving keep Japan has only 12 "surviving keeps" left (original castle towers from the Edo period or earlier that have survived without being destroyed by war or disaster), and only 5 of them are designated national treasures: Himeji Castle, Matsumoto Castle, Inuyama Castle, Hikone Castle and Matsue Castle. Himeji Castle isn't just one of them, it's also the largest and most structurally complex. It was once sold off at a low price and nearly torn down for building materials, escaping only because demolition would have cost too much, and then it also survived the war. What we see today was completed in the early 17th century, more than 400 years ago. In terms of modern architecture, the height between the castle's floors is like a double-height space, and around the edges there are small platforms you have to climb a few steps to reach, designed for watching and defense. The stairs between floors even have doors that can be shut downward toward the floor. If you're also the kind of person who gets especially excited about structure and details like stairs, Himeji Castle might make you forget the time. Compared with the other national-treasure castles, Hikone and Inuyama, Himeji is really in a completely different league in scale. Admission is 2,500 yen per person, open 9:00 to 17:00. Engyoji on Mount Shosha: the "Mount Hiei of the West" Engyoji was founded in 966 and is a special head temple (bekkaku honzan) of the Tendai sect. Because of its deep ties to Mount Hiei, it's called the "Mount Hiei of the West", and its standing and scale are among the top in the Kansai area. It's also the 27th temple of the Saigoku 33 Kannon Pilgrimage, and was once a filming location for the movie The Last Samurai. From the view on the ropeway ride up the mountain, to strolling the grounds and looking at the temple buildings, it's perfect for slowing down. I went on a weekday afternoon and stayed two hours, and met fewer than 50 people the whole time, so it was very peaceful. Admission 500 yen per person, ropeway round trip another 1,200 yen per person, open 8:30 to 18:00 (until 17:00 in winter) Tendai sect: founded in the early 9th century by the master Saicho in the Heian period. Although it originates from Mount Tiantai in China, in Japan it developed a unique system combining "the perfect teaching, esoteric Buddhism, Zen and the precepts", with Enryakuji on Mount Hiei as the head temple. In Japan today, Tendai believers may be fewer than those of the Jodo or Shingon sects, but nearly all the founders of the Kamakura new Buddhism (Jodo, Jodo Shinshu, Zen, Nichiren and so on) came from Mount Hiei, so Mount Hiei is seen as the cross-sectarian "mother mountain of Japanese Buddhism", with a very high standing in scholarship, culture and history. Jikido (dining hall): where monks used to live and eat during their training. (Important Cultural Property of Japan) Nada no Kenka Matsuri: the "fighting festival" that draws tens of thousands of pilgrims The autumn grand festival of Matsubara Hachiman Shrine, "Nada no Kenka Matsuri" (灘のけんか祭り), is held every year on 10/14 to 15, and is the biggest festival I've ever taken part in. The Japanese word "kenka" (喧嘩) literally means "fight", and the core of the festival is carrying mikoshi (portable shrines) and festival floats and smashing them into each other. Day one: Yoimiya (the eve festival) At 11 in the morning, the floats (yatai) of seven villages set out on a parade from their own villages, then gather together at the shrine. The afternoon "neriawase" is the peak of the day: first they collide in the plaza in front of the shrine's two-story gate, villages competing and showing off their might. Then they move inside the shrine to collide as a ritual offering performed for the gods, presenting unity and strength as tribute. Finally, the grand neriawase in the plaza is a free-for-all of "so satisfying! (?)". Collisions inside the shrine These floats are finely made like works of art and cost a fortune, so the so-called collisions are actually "gentleman's collisions", touching without really hitting, with a commander blowing a whistle and raising a flag to signal two floats to separate, like calling boxers back to their corners in a boxing match. Before a collision starts, two blocks of wood are struck together with a crisp sound, like a "ready... get ready~" warning. ＊The floats (also translated as "mountain carts") carried by each village are called "yatai (屋台)" in Japanese. They're mobile stages for offering performances to the gods. No god sits inside, but 4 people who beat the taiko and control the rhythm, called "norikoshi (乗子)", usually boys aged 10 to 15, symbolizing the village's future and purity. During the festival their feet can't touch the ground, and someone has to be holding them the whole time. The mikoshi, which do carry a god, are called "mikoshi (神輿)" in Japanese. Day two: Honmiya, the "for real!" collisions At 6 in the morning there's a purification ritual at the seaside, ending around 6:20, for the people who will carry the mikoshi that day. The mikoshi look similar to the floats but plainer, and a god is really enshrined inside: Emperor Ojin, Empress Jingu and Himegami, in three mikoshi (Ichinomaru, Ninomaru and Sannomaru). And the mikoshi collisions really do send wood chips flying. The purification ritual at 6 a.m. At 11 in the morning, the mikoshi first have a round of collisions in the plaza in front of the shrine and inside the shrine. The space is small so you can watch up close, and it's said to be quite shocking. At 2 p.m., the procession moves to the practice ground at the foot of Otabiyama for a second round of collisions. This practice ground is as huge as giant stairs, and only when you see it with your own eyes do you understand that the "tens of thousands of participants" in the info isn't an exaggeration. The picnic-style seats on the steps are hereditary, so ordinary visitors can only stand on top of Otabiyama and look from afar, taking in the crowd filling the whole stepped stand at the same time, which is also a highlight for visitors. A super huge stepped grandstand Around 4 in the evening, the mikoshi and floats climb Otabiyama together. The final steep stretch is about 400 to 500 meters. The info says the mikoshi weigh at least 300 kg and the floats 2 tons, so this last mile is the ultimate test of endurance for those carrying. ＊The festival has a special verb "neru (練る)", meaning "to shout chants (like "Yoiyasa"), sway the mikoshi in rhythm and stride forward full of spirit". The preparation before carrying is swaying back and forth to build up momentum, which, besides using leverage physically, also carries a sense of provoking and intimidating the other side. Floats going back into storage: another kind of solemnity beyond the excitement If you happen to pass by the shrine during the festival, you might also see the floats being put back into their storage houses (yataigura). The atmosphere is solemn and careful, but not stern. It's not an exciting moment, but you can feel how much the locals value tradition. The storage house is small and the float can't go straight in, so before it goes in, you'll see the onion-shaped metal ornament at the top, the "giboshi", taken off, and the carved wooden base below it, the "roban", carried down the stairs on someone's head. The giant ropes hanging from the four corners, the "datezuna", are also pulled taut and fixed. Giboshi (擬宝珠): the metal ornament at the very tip of the float. Roban (露盤): the delicate carved wooden base below the giboshi, usually carved with scenes of slaying evil dragons, historical heroes or myths, weighing 20 to 30 kg. Datezuna (伊達綱): giant twisted ropes hanging at the four corners of the float, made of precious brocade thread and gold thread, usually with gorgeous gold tassels at the ends. They're a symbol of the village's wealth, and how beautifully and forcefully they swing is also used to judge how well the float is being carried. Taking down the roban Moon viewing and the pottery fair: seasonal events around Himeji Castle The Himeji Castle moon viewing (Mid-Autumn Festival, the 15th of the lunar month) is a free event. Himeji Castle is lit up, there are stage performances, and people can find a spot on the lawn for a picnic. There are also local sake stalls, and I bought a set of "plastic cup + 3 pours of sake" for 700 yen, on an "honor system" basis: you take your cup to the stall and fill it up yourself, and the staff usually fill it to the brim. I saw Japanese people bringing food containers to fill with sake, clearly well prepared. That was how it was in 2025, and I don't know if it's the same every year. The local sake stall at the Himeji Castle moon viewing The National Pottery Fair (early November) is held in the plaza of Otemae Park in front of Himeji Castle, and every prefecture's "○○-yaki" sets up a stall. Prices aren't especially high and it leans toward the general public, with relatively fewer pieces from small studios, but seeing all kinds of local specialty pottery in one place is still well worth a visit. It's quite crowded, a bit shoulder to shoulder. I bought a grater Himeji food: seasonal local produce Autumn catch from the Seto Inland Sea Himeji faces the Seto Inland Sea and has a rich catch, and I bought everything at the supermarket "Halows". Sardines (真鰯): small fish you eat bones and all. Many of the small-fish dishes you eat in Japan are this. Red tongue sole (赤舌ひらめ): both eyes on the same side, with delicate flesh, and simply simmered in sauce it's really good. Barracuda (カマス): the texture is a bit like tilapia but softer, with a narrow body but thick flesh. Rabbitfish (バリ／アイゴ): the skin is smooth as if it has no scales. Be careful, since the dorsal, anal and pelvic fins all have venomous spines, so you have to handle it with care. Pacific saury (秋刀魚): 2025 was called a "once in ten years" fat year, and simply pan-fried it's pure happiness. Shirasa shrimp (シラサエビ): it's rare to see shrimp in a Japanese supermarket that are fresh, head-on, and still moving! Swimming crab (渡り蟹): not only cheap but really tasty, my top recommendation as a representative crab. I even found it tastier than the matsuba crab I ate by the Sea of Japan! It's around 1,000 yen (depending on size), and when it's half price it's so cheap you want to cry and still fresh. Just steamed it's sweet and fresh with plenty of meat, super satisfying! Fish and shrimp I bought at the supermarket Sardines (真鰯) Autumn fruits and vegetables Grapes: Because of geography, the grapes you buy in western Hyogo, where Himeji is, mostly come from Okayama (though Japan's highest-producing and best-known grape region is actually Yamanashi!). I ate five, six, seven, eight kinds, but the one I recommend most is the everywhere-you-look, uniquely fragrant "Shine Muscat" (シャインマスカット). It's usually green, but at the farm co-op supermarket "JA Hyogo Nishi Shunsaigura Shosha" I found a paler green variety, even with a pink-purple gradient, that was even better than the green one, so amazing! I ate a lot of varieties, but I'm no expert and don't remember much about them, so please go and buy some yourself~ Generally speaking, green grapes can nearly all be eaten with the skin on, and most are seedless. ＊I bought most of mine at a local shop called "Sanchi Chokusou Furubejipo", which had more than ten varieties at the time, so many Shine Muscat grown in Himeji Oriental Star: grown in small quantities around Japan, oval-shaped, can be eaten with the skin but the skin is noticeable. Other grape varieties Persimmons: persimmons are also an autumn fruit, and there are so many persimmon trees along the roads, full of fruit, giving you wicked thoughts. Later a Japanese person told me "you can pick them freely~", so I tried picking at a spot where the persimmon tree didn't seem to belong to anyone, and they were as good as the ones you pay for! The most common is Fuyu, and there's also Fude persimmon. When you cut open a Fude persimmon the inside is a dark orange that looks like it's gone bad, and that's normal. If you see houses drying persimmons, they're mostly astringent varieties (like "Mino persimmon / shibugaki") meant only for drying and can't be eaten raw, and farm co-op supermarkets usually label them with a warning. A Fude persimmon that looks like it's gone bad Taishu persimmon Chestnuts: the chestnuts common in Japan are big. Sometimes you run into little stalls roasting chestnuts, and the thin astringent skin clinging to the flesh is super hard to peel. Japanese people said you can eat it with the skin and don't need to peel it clean. Water bamboo and a giant pumpkin Conclusion Himeji Castle + Engyoji are a must. A quick trip could do one in the morning and one in the afternoon (2 to 3 hours each), but I'm old, and I can only fit one thing into a day. If you happen to go in mid-October, I strongly recommend watching the "Nada no Kenka Matsuri", and the transport is convenient too. Autumn really is the season of appetite, and not seriously eating the seasonal local produce would be a disservice to yourself.

title: Shodoshima on the Seto Inland Sea, with No Art Festival
abstract: On my way to my next work-exchange spot in Himeji, I stopped by Shodoshima: a three-hour ferry from Himeji Port, a cozy guesthouse, and a soy sauce factory and sake brewery, and only then did I realize it wasn't art festival season at all.
text: Before heading to my next work-exchange spot (Himeji), the Setouchi Triennale was on this year for the first time in a while, so I stopped by Shodoshima for a trip. I'd never taken a ferry and wanted to try one. I'd planned to leave from Kobe and even considered an overnight sailing to save on accommodation, but it happened to be on a ferry maintenance day, so I switched to leaving from Himeji Port, a 3-hour trip. Buses on Shodoshima aren't very frequent, and I had to transfer too, so I left Himeji by boat a bit after 11 and didn't reach my lodging on Shodoshima until 4 or 5 in the afternoon. Sen Guesthouse The place I chose is a home that doubles as a guesthouse, with a kitchen, a living room and a balcony, decorated very cozily, and there's even a hammock by the sea a short walk away. The dorm room had only 4 beds, and I wasn't bothered by roommates at all these days, so it was very peaceful and comfortable. Having just come off a week of nonstop, intense socializing, cooking and wandering around at random were truly the best rest for me. Making breakfast and dinner for myself every day, and even going out on trips, felt too heavy for me these days. On my last evening I met another guest, a Brazilian girl named Hanna, and we soaked our feet, shared dinner and said goodbye to Shodoshima together. Another day, while waiting for a bus, an elderly couple who had retired and moved to Shodoshima gave me a ride. Thank you to the lovely, kind people of once-in-a-lifetime encounters. Notes From about 4,000 yen per person Near the Twenty-Four Eyes Movie Village, and rather hard to reach (though you can ask the bus driver to stop at the guesthouse door, which is already very convenient). You also have to climb about two stories of stairs to get to the house. Update: this summer (2026) they actually installed a cargo lift on the stairs...! @senguesthouse It's not art festival season, huh The funny thing is that only on the night I arrived, while planning where to go the next day, did I realize it wasn't the art festival period at all right then. (The Setouchi Triennale has spring, summer and autumn sessions, with a stretch of non-exhibition time between each.) It was a total blunder, but there were more places to go than I expected (though some spots I found pretty ordinary), and I didn't even go to the farther parts of the island (I was really tired). I visited all the sightseeing spots I should have, but what I liked most was still wandering through small alleys and zoning out. Meiro no Machi and the Angel Road It's in Tonosho, next to the "Dobuchi Strait". As a lover of poking around narrow alleys, I really liked it! This area has some festival art sites (though they were all closed when I went), plus quite a few restaurants and cafés, good for eating and resting. On the way to the seaside spot "Angel Road", I also liked passing Saiko-ji Temple (in May 2026 they welcomed a branch image of Mazu from Beigang Chaotian Temple! So cool!), where you can look out over the town and the sea from above. Twenty-Four Eyes Movie Village and Olive Park Twenty-Four Eyes Movie Village: a village built for filming a movie and then kept, where you can feel the atmosphere of an early Showa fishing village. I'd already been to quite a few rural places and different kinds of buildings, so it was only moderately appealing to me. Shodoshima Olive Park: good for photos and buying all kinds of souvenirs. About 80% of the visitors are (Taiwanese-speaking) Taiwanese XD It was a filming location for the live-action Kiki's Delivery Service, so there are some facilities for taking photos, and you can rent (magic) brooms for free. Notes Twenty-Four Eyes Movie Village: 8:30 to 17:00, 1,000 yen per person Shodoshima Olive Park: 8:30 to 17:00 Yamaroku wooden-barrel soy sauce For food on Shodoshima, the main specialties are olive oil, somen and soy sauce. I had the olive oil, somen and soy sauce flavors of soft-serve ice cream. The soy sauce one I had at "Yamaroku Shoyu": it's just regular milk flavor with soy sauce poured right on top plus black beans, but surprisingly it goes well together, and I liked it! They even give you a jar of soy sauce to use freely. They brew soy sauce the traditional way in giant barrels made of cedar. You can go inside to look, take photos with the barrels, and there's a simple tour, all free, so when you leave there's a pressure of "I guess I should buy some soy sauce" (I'm thin-skinned...), but I still thought it was well worth it, and that keeping traditions alive really isn't easy. Notes 9:00 to 17:00 20 minutes on foot from the bus stop, soy sauce products from 750 yen. It's a big Japanese-style house, and you can have an ice cream and rest. Moriguni Sake Brewery Another place worth noting is Shodoshima's only sake brewery, "Moriguni Sake Brewery". I came because I really wanted somewhere to rest and there weren't many options (so casual!). By the time I arrived it was 4 in the afternoon, and I only had a cup of sake and a dessert, and sadly didn't get to try the sake lees bread and the food. But the atmosphere was nice (and I was the only customer...!), and I got a great rest. Notes 9:00 to 17:00, closed Thursdays; the bakery is closed Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday Somebody please try their bread on my behalf!!! Wrap-up Overall, the three or four days on Shodoshima were very chill, and the cozy hostel gave me a great first impression. The sights on the island are some very touristy, some very traditional and some natural, and every day you see a different sea view from a different angle. Recommended. (Poor vocabulary.)
